rows.label: P7 · PROPOSAL · the why of the swearing
rows.text: Your little one might say it's you. You don't have to accept every conclusion they reach about you, but do listen for the concrete complaint without fighting the yelling and swearing around it. If it's something serious, answer it seriously. The complaint might only be one sentence, once the swearing runs out. Like the anger at bedtime, the swearing is there to get them heard, so once you're listening instead of fighting, they don't need it anymore.

rows.label: P8 · PROPOSAL · why he can do it
rows.text: You can see the same move in a dramatized scene from the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers it must not have been easy for his sons to grow up with him as a father. He doesn't collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what's worth answering in it. He agrees with Lloyd, talks honestly about both of his sons, and thanks him for the perspective. Like the two truths at bedtime, a true complaint and real love don't cancel each other out, so you can take the true part without giving up your love or defending yourself.
